job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

passage: In a lively Class 7 social studies discussion, Ms. Sharma explained the core of Indian democracy. 'Students,' she began, 'our Constitution ensures that every adult citizen has an equal right to vote, regardless of their wealth or social status.' Rahul asked, 'But teacher, does a billionaire’s vote carry more weight than a poor person’s vote?' Ms. Sharma smiled and replied, 'No, Rahul. In the eyes of the law, every citizen’s vote is equal.' Priya then raised a concern about social barriers. 'What about private businesses? Can a shopkeeper refuse service to someone based on their caste?' Ms. Sharma shook her head firmly. 'Absolutely not. The Constitution prohibits discrimination in public places, including private shops that serve the public. Equality before the law means no one can be denied access based on their background.' Finally, the class discussed the Mid-day Meal scheme. 'Is this program just to feed hungry children?' asked Rahul. Ms. Sharma clarified, 'While it provides nutrition, its primary goal is to promote social equality by bringing children from all backgrounds together to eat in the same classroom, breaking down deep-seated caste prejudices.' The students realized that democracy is not just about voting, but about ensuring dignity and fairness for everyone in daily life.

items.evidence: 'Students,' she began, 'our Constitution ensures that every adult citizen has an equal right to vote, regardless of their wealth or social status.'
items.q: Kamla is a poor adult farmer who cannot read. What is true about her vote?
options: She has the same right to vote as anyone
She can vote only after learning to read
She can vote only if her family owns land
She can vote only in her village council
items.explain: Every adult citizen has an equal right to vote, whatever their wealth or social status.

wrong.why: thinks only literate people can vote
thinks only landowning families can vote
thinks poor people get only a limited vote

items.evidence: In the eyes of the law, every citizen’s vote is equal.
items.q: A factory owner and his worker vote for different candidates. How are their votes counted?
options: Both votes count exactly the same
The owner's vote counts more than the worker's
The one in more committees gets extra votes
Only the landowning owner's vote is counted
items.explain: In the eyes of the law, every citizen's vote is equal, rich or poor.

wrong.why: thinks rich people's votes count more
thinks belonging to more groups gives more votes

items.evidence: The Constitution prohibits discrimination in public places, including private shops that serve the public.
items.q: A private sweet shop owner turns away a customer because of her caste. Is this allowed?
options: Not allowed, because the shop serves the public
Allowed, because the shop is privately owned
Allowed, if the local community agrees to it
Not allowed, but only in government buildings
items.explain: The ban on discrimination covers private shops too, because they serve the public.

wrong.why: thinks private shops can refuse people by caste
thinks community agreement allows caste separation
thinks the rule covers only government places

items.evidence: Equality before the law means no one can be denied access based on their background.
items.q: Which example at a hotel best shows equality before the law?
options: Guests of every caste may enter and eat
Every guest gets exactly the same dish and bill
Ministers' families may enter before other guests
Guests of some castes eat in a separate room
items.explain: Equality before the law means nobody can be denied access because of their background.

wrong.why: thinks equality means identical treatment in everything
thinks officials are above the law
thinks separate spaces for castes are fair

items.evidence: Ms. Sharma clarified, 'While it provides nutrition, its primary goal is to promote social equality by bringing children from all backgrounds together to eat in the same classroom, breaking down deep-seated caste prejudices.'
items.q: Why do children of all castes eat the mid-day meal together in one classroom?
options: To weaken caste prejudice among children
To feed hungry children, nothing more
To prove caste discrimination has fully ended
To give every child exactly equal portions
items.explain: Eating together brings children of all backgrounds close and breaks down caste prejudices.

wrong.why: thinks the meal is only about food
thinks the meal means discrimination has ended
